title: Genesis 31. The Cup of the Return.
edition: AID Genesis, Layer 1 (the steward's manuscript); narration: Kristin voice (public domain)
level_note: text follows the narration phrase by phrase
verse_numbers: none in this text; none shown
phrases: Genesis 31. The Cup of the Return.
Jacob heard the words of Laban's sons:
Jacob has taken away all that was our father's.
From what was our father's, he has gained all this wealth.
And Jacob saw the expression on Laban's face, and behold,
it was not toward him as before.
The welcome has worn thin.
The uncle who ran to meet him, embraced him, kissed him,
now looks at him differently.
The flocks that were Laban's are Jacob's.
The sons that are Laban's daughters' are Jacob's.
The wealth that was Laban's has crossed to Jacob's side.
And Laban's sons have noticed.
The Lord said to Jacob:
Return to the land of your fathers and to your kindred,
and I will be with you.
return.
The same word God has used since the beginning.
Abraham was told to go, Each generation receives a different.
Jacob is told return.
Isaac was told to sojourn.
movement word.
The Cup moves out, stays, returns.
The promise that was carried out of Canaan into Haran is now called back.
The dream at Bethel, I will bring you back to this land,
begins to draw.
Jacob sends and calls Rachel and Leah to the field,
to his flock.
He tells them everything.
I see that your father's face is not toward me as before.
But the God of my father has been with me.
You know that I have served your father with all my strength.
Your father has deceived me and changed my wages ten times,
but God did not allow him to hurt me.
He tells them about the dream.
The angel of God said: Jacob.
Here I am.
Lift up your eyes and see,
all the male goats that leap on the flock are streaked, speckled,
and grizzled, for I have seen all that Laban does to you.
I am the God of Bethel, where you anointed a pillar,
where you vowed a vow to Me.
Now arise, get out from this land,
and return to the land of your birth.
Bethel.
The place where Jacob slept on a stone and saw a stairway.
The place where he said if.
The place where he poured oil on a pillar and named it the House of God.
God calls him back to that place, not physically yet,
but in memory.
The God of Bethel is the God who appeared to a man who had nothing and gave him everything.
Now He says: the time has come to go home.
Rachel and Leah answered:
Is there any portion or inheritance for us in our father's house?
Are we not regarded by him as foreigners?
For he has sold us and has used up our money.
All the wealth that God has taken away from our father is ours and our children's.
Now then, whatever God has said to you, do.
The wives choose.
The same word Rebekah spoke, I will go,
now echoes through her daughters-in-law.
Whatever God has said to you, do.
The women who were traded, sold, given, bargained for,
now speak as free agents.
The Cup that was carried into Haran by a man with a stone pillow is now carried out by a household that agrees to go.
Jacob rose up and set his sons and wives on camels.
He took all his livestock and all his possessions,
which he had gained in Paddan-aram,
to go to Isaac his father in the land of Canaan.
The return begins.
The man who left with nothing now leaves with everything.
Two wives.
Eleven sons.
One daughter.
Flocks.
Servants.
Camels.
Donkeys.
The Cup that was carried out empty is now carried back full.
The promise that went out as a dream returns as a household.
But Laban had gone to shear his sheep.
And Rachel stole the teraphim that were her father's.
The teraphim.
Household gods.
Idols.
The beloved wife, the one Jacob worked fourteen years for,
the one God remembered, the one who named Joseph,
may the Lord add,
takes false gods when she leaves her father's house.
The woman who said whatever God has said to you, do,
also steals her father's gods.
The Cup of the covenant is now carrying idols inside it.
The vessel that holds the promise is also holding something that is not the promise.
Jacob did not know.
He left with everything, crossing the Euphrates,
heading toward the hill country of Gilead.
The man who deceived his father is now deceived by his wife.
The same pattern, the deceiver deceived,
follows him out of Haran as it followed him in.
Laban was told on the third day that Jacob had fled.
He took his relatives and pursued him seven days' journey.
He overtook him in the mountains of Gilead.
But God came to Laban the Syrian in a dream by night and said:
Be careful that you do not speak to Jacob either good or bad.
The same God who came to Abimelech in a dream now comes to Laban.
The God of the covenant intervenes in the dreams of those who do not carry the covenant.
The Cup is protected, not by Jacob's courage, not by Rachel's cunning,
by God speaking to the one who pursues.
Laban caught up with Jacob.
He said: What have you done,
that you have deceived me and carried away my daughters like captives of the sword?
Why did you flee secretly and deceive me, and not tell me,
that I might have sent you away with mirth and songs,
with tambourine and harp?
You did not allow me to kiss my sons and daughters.
You have done foolishly.
It is in the power of my hand to hurt you,
but the God of your father spoke to me last night, saying,
Be careful that you do not speak to Jacob either good or bad.
Laban claims he would have sent them with joy.
The uncle who deceived Jacob with Leah,
who changed his wages ten times,
who removed the speckled flocks before the deal could take effect,
now says he would have thrown a party.
The same self-justification that has run through every deceiver in Genesis.
But even Laban admits: your God warned me.
Then he asks the question he really came for:
Why have you stolen my gods?
Jacob answered: Because I was afraid, for I said,
Lest you should take your daughters from me by force.
Anyone you find your gods with shall not live.
Before our relatives, discern what is yours with me, and take it.
Jacob does not know Rachel stole them.
He pronounces a death sentence on the thief,
unknowingly sentencing his own beloved wife.
The man who said if at Bethel, who served fourteen years,
who schemed with rods, now speaks a curse he does not understand.
The Cup of the covenant carries a hidden lie,
and the vessel does not know it.
Laban went into Jacob's tent, into Leah's tent,
into the tent of the two female servants.
He did not find them.
He went out of Leah's tent and entered into Rachel's tent.
Now Rachel had taken the teraphim, put them in the camel's saddle,
and sat on them.
Laban felt around all the tent but did not find them.
She said to her father:
Let not my lord be angry that I cannot rise up before you,
for the way of women is upon me.
He searched but did not find the teraphim.
She lies while sitting on the gods.
The beloved wife, the one God remembered, the one who named Joseph,
uses her body as a seat for idols and her mouth to deceive her father.
The same pattern as Jacob deceiving Isaac, a daughter deceiving a father.
The same darkness.
The same flesh used to hide the truth.
The Cup of the covenant has a lie sitting on top of false gods,
inside the beloved wife's tent,
in the household that is carrying the promise home.
Jacob was angry and argued with Laban.
He answered: What is my trespass?
What is my sin, that you have hotly pursued me?
Now that you have felt around in all my stuff,
what have you found of all your household stuff?
Set it here before my relatives and your relatives,
that they may judge between us two.
These twenty years I have been with you.
Your ewes and your female goats have not cast their young,
and I have not eaten the rams of your flocks.
What was torn by animals I did not bring to you.
I bore the loss.
Of my hand you required it,
whether stolen by day or stolen by night.
This was my situation: in the day the drought consumed me,
and the frost by night.
My sleep fled from my eyes.
These twenty years I have been in your house.
I served you fourteen years for your two daughters,
and six years for your flock,
and you have changed my wages ten times.
Unless the God of my father,
the God of Abraham and the Fear of Isaac,
had been with me,
surely now you would have sent me away empty.
God has seen my affliction and the labor of my hands,
and rebuked you last night.
Twenty years.
The man who grabbed a heel and stole a blessing now speaks of labor.
Heat and frost.
Sleepless nights.
Ewes that did not miscarry.
Rams he did not eat.
Losses he bore himself.
The Cup of labor has been poured out for two decades,
and the vessel that poured it is angry.
Not the anger of a grabber.
The anger of a man who has been deceived, cheated, and pursued,
and who knows that without God he would have nothing.
He names God three times.
The God of my father.
The God of Abraham.
The Fear of Isaac.
The covenant is named across three generations, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob,
in a single breath.
The Cup that was given to the first is now claimed by the third.
The God who was the God of my father is now my God,
because He was with me.
Laban answered: The daughters are my daughters.
The children are my children.
The flocks are my flocks.
All that you see is mine.
But what can I do today about these my daughters,
or about their children whom they have borne?
Laban claims everything.
The same uncle who sold his daughters, who changed wages,
who removed flocks, now says: everything is mine.
But he also admits: I cannot do anything about it.
The Cup has crossed the line.
The promise has left Haran.
The vessel is beyond his reach.
Now come, let us make a covenant, you and I.
Let it be a witness between me and you.
Jacob took a stone and set it up as a pillar.
He said to his relatives: Gather stones.
They took stones and made a heap.
They ate there by the heap.
Laban called it Jegar-sahadutha, Witness Heap in Aramaic.
Jacob called it Galeed, Witness Heap in Hebrew.
The same gesture as Abraham and Abimelech at Beersheba.
The same covenant between men who do not trust each other.
The same heap of stones.
The same meal.
But where Abraham and Abimelech made peace,
Jacob and Laban make a boundary.
This is not friendship.
It is separation.
Laban said: This heap is a witness between me and you today.
Therefore it was named Galeed, and Mizpah, for he said:
The Lord watch between you and me,
when we are absent one from another.
If you afflict my daughters,
or if you take wives in addition to my daughters,
no man is with us.
Behold, God is witness between me and you.
Mizpah.
Watch.
The covenant of suspicion.
The Lord watch between you and me.
A boundary made of stones and distrust.
The Cup that was carried out of Haran is now marked by a heap that says:
do not cross this line.
The uncle and the nephew part with a witness between them,
not of love but of guardedness.
Jacob swore by the Fear of his father Isaac.
He offered a sacrifice in the mountain and called his relatives to eat bread.
They ate bread and stayed all night in the mountain.
Early in the morning,
Laban rose up and kissed his sons and daughters and blessed them.
Laban departed and returned to his place.
The kiss.
The same kiss Jacob's father gave Esau, or did not give.
The same kiss Laban gave Jacob when he first arrived.
Now Laban kisses his daughters and grandchildren and leaves.
The uncle who deceived, the father-in-law who changed wages,
the man who pursued seven days, goes home.
The Cup is free of him.
The promise is moving toward the land.
But inside the Cup, hidden under the camel's saddle,
inside the beloved wife's tent, are the teraphim.
False gods.
Stolen.
Hidden.
Lied about.
The Cup is full.
It is moving home.
And it is carrying something that does not belong in it.
The vessel does not know.
The man who carried the promise for twenty years does not know his wife has idols in her saddle.
The God who appeared at Bethel, who said return,
who warned Laban in a dream, does not remove them.
The Cup is carried forward, full, returning, and mixed.
The promise and the idols travel together.
The covenant and the lie ride the same camel.
The God who sees does not yet expose what is hidden.
But He will.
The Cup must be poured through a fire that separates what belongs in it from what does not.
That fire is coming.
Its name is Peniel.
